description: Design a real-time operating system task architecture from system requirements through schedulability analysis. Covers priority assignment (rate monotonic and deadline monotonic), utilization bound testing, response time analysis, inter-task communication design, stack sizing, and interrupt latency budgeting.

steps.description: Decompose system requirements into RTOS tasks by identifying periodic, aperiodic, and sporadic workloads, then assigning each a rate and worst-case execution time.

inputs.name: system-requirements
inputs.desc: Functional and timing requirements for the embedded system

inputs.name: hardware-platform
inputs.desc: Target MCU/MPU with clock speed, interrupt controller type, and available peripherals

outputs.name: task-list
outputs.desc: Each task with name, type (periodic/aperiodic/sporadic), period or minimum inter-arrival time in ms, and measured or estimated WCET

outputs.name: isr-list
outputs.desc: Each interrupt source with worst-case execution time and triggering frequency

process: List every stimulus the system must respond to: sensor reads, communication frames, user inputs, timer expirations, and actuator updates.

Classify each stimulus as periodic (fixed interval), sporadic (minimum inter-arrival time known), or aperiodic (no guaranteed minimum interval). Aperiodic stimuli need a server task (polling or deferrable server).
For each periodic stimulus, record the period T in ms. For sporadic, record the minimum inter-arrival time. These become the task periods.

Measure or estimate worst-case execution time (WCET) for each task on the target hardware. Use instrumented code with GPIO toggling and an oscilloscope for measurement. For estimates, count instructions in the longest path and divide by clock cycles per instruction.
Group related stimuli into a single task only when they share the same period and can tolerate the combined WCET. Otherwise keep them separate.

List hardware interrupts separately. Each ISR should do minimal work: read the hardware register, clear the flag, post to a queue or set an event flag, then return. The deferred processing goes in a task.

steps.description: Assign task priorities using rate monotonic analysis or deadline monotonic scheduling, then verify with utilization bound and exact response time tests.

inputs.name: task-list
inputs.desc: Tasks with periods and WCETs

inputs.name: isr-list
inputs.desc: Interrupts with WCETs and frequencies

outputs.name: priority-table
outputs.desc: Each task with assigned priority level, period, WCET, and utilization

outputs.name: schedulability-result
outputs.desc: Pass/fail with utilization sum, utilization bound, and per-task response times vs deadlines

process: Calculate utilization for each task: U_i = C_i / T_i where C_i is WCET and T_i is period. Sum all utilizations to get total U.

For rate monotonic scheduling (RMS), assign higher priority to shorter-period tasks. For deadline monotonic (DMS), assign higher priority to shorter-deadline tasks. RMS is optimal for implicit deadlines (D = T). DMS is optimal when deadlines differ from periods.

Check the Liu and Layland utilization bound: U_bound = n * (2^(1/n) - 1) for n tasks. If total U is less than or equal to U_bound, the task set is schedulable under RMS. This is a sufficient but not necessary condition.

For task sets that exceed the utilization bound but have U less than 1.0, perform exact response time analysis. For each task i: R_i = C_i + sum over higher priority j of ceiling(R_i / T_j) * C_j. Iterate until R_i converges. If R_i is less than or equal to D_i for all tasks, the system is schedulable.
Account for ISR overhead in the response time analysis by treating interrupt processing time as the highest-priority 'task' that preempts everything.

If schedulability fails, options in order of preference: reduce WCET through code optimization, increase the processor clock, move to a faster MCU, or relax the deadline requirements with the system architect.

steps.description: Design inter-task communication using queues, semaphores, mutexes with priority inheritance, and event flags, choosing the right mechanism for each data flow.

inputs.name: priority-table
inputs.desc: Tasks with assigned priorities

inputs.name: task-list
inputs.desc: Tasks with their data dependencies and shared resources

outputs.name: ipc-architecture
outputs.desc: Each IPC object (queue, mutex, semaphore, event group) with connected tasks, data type, and size

outputs.name: blocking-analysis
outputs.desc: Maximum blocking time each task can experience from lower-priority tasks holding shared resources

process: Map every data flow between tasks. Producer-consumer flows use message queues. Shared resource access uses mutexes. Synchronization points use binary semaphores or event flags.

Size each message queue: depth = burst rate * processing latency / message period. Add margin for jitter. The queue depth determines how much memory the RTOS allocates and how long the system can tolerate a processing delay without data loss.

For every shared resource (hardware peripheral, global data structure, flash memory), assign a mutex. Always use mutexes with priority inheritance or priority ceiling protocol to prevent unbounded priority inversion.

Calculate worst-case blocking time B_i for each task: the longest critical section of any lower-priority task that shares a resource with task i. This blocking term adds to the response time equation: R_i = C_i + B_i + sum of preemption from higher-priority tasks.
Use event flag groups when a task must wait for multiple conditions (e.g., sensor data ready AND calibration complete). This avoids nested semaphore waits that can deadlock.

Design a deadlock prevention strategy: impose a global lock ordering. If task A acquires mutex 1 then mutex 2, every task must acquire them in the same order. Document the lock ordering in the design.

steps.description: Determine stack size for each RTOS task and the ISR stack using call graph analysis, local variable accounting, and runtime painting verification.

inputs.name: ipc-architecture
inputs.desc: IPC objects and their memory requirements

inputs.name: priority-table
inputs.desc: Tasks with priorities for preemption analysis

outputs.name: stack-allocation-table
outputs.desc: Each task's stack size in bytes with breakdown: call depth, locals, RTOS overhead, safety margin

outputs.name: memory-budget
outputs.desc: Total RAM usage: task stacks, ISR stack, RTOS kernel objects, message queue buffers, and heap (if used)

process: For each task, build the call graph from the task entry function. Tools like GCC's -fstack-usage flag produce per-function stack usage. Sum the stack usage along the deepest call path.
Add the RTOS context save overhead: for ARM Cortex-M, this is 32 bytes for the hardware-stacked registers plus whatever the RTOS pushes (typically 32 to 64 more bytes for software context).

Add ISR preemption overhead. When an ISR preempts a task, the hardware stacks 8 registers (32 bytes on Cortex-M). Nested interrupts stack again. The ISR stack (separate on Cortex-M with RTOS support via MSP/PSP split) handles this.
Size the ISR stack: sum the worst-case nesting depth times the per-interrupt frame size. Most systems allow 2 to 4 levels of nesting.

Add a safety margin of 25% to each calculated stack. This covers compiler optimizations that change call depth, floating point context (additional 72 bytes on Cortex-M4F), and library functions with stack-heavy implementations.

Verify at runtime using stack painting: fill each stack with a known pattern (0xDEADBEEF) at startup, then periodically check how much of the pattern remains. The high-water mark should stay at least 15% below the allocated size. If not, increase the stack.

steps.description: Verify the RTOS design meets all timing requirements through instrumented measurement, logic analyzer capture, and systematic deadline compliance testing.

inputs.name: stack-allocation-table
inputs.desc: Finalized stack allocations

inputs.name: schedulability-result
inputs.desc: Theoretical analysis results to compare against measured values

outputs.name: timing-report
outputs.desc: Measured vs theoretical response times, worst-case latencies, jitter measurements, and pass/fail per requirement

outputs.name: rtos-configuration
outputs.desc: Final RTOS config: tick rate, priority levels used, kernel objects, memory pool sizes, and configuration macros

process: Instrument each task: toggle a GPIO pin high at task entry, low at task exit. Capture with a logic analyzer over a long run (hours). Measure maximum execution time, period jitter, and response time from stimulus to completion.
Compare measured WCET against the values used in schedulability analysis. If measured WCET exceeds the estimate, rerun the response time analysis with corrected values.

Select the RTOS tick rate. Common choices: 1 kHz (1 ms resolution) for most systems, 10 kHz for sub-ms timing needs. Higher tick rates increase ISR overhead. The tick ISR itself must be the shortest ISR in the system.

Test corner cases: simultaneous arrival of all periodic tasks (critical instant), maximum burst of sporadic events, all queues at capacity. These stress tests reveal failures that normal operation hides.

Measure interrupt latency: time from interrupt assertion to first ISR instruction. On Cortex-M with zero-latency interrupts, this is 12 clock cycles minimum. RTOS critical sections add to this. Verify the measured value meets the hardware timing requirements.

Document the final configuration: RTOS version, tick rate, number of priority levels, each kernel object (tasks, queues, mutexes, semaphores, event groups, timers) with its parameters. This becomes the RTOS design record for the project.

description: Design an interrupt architecture for an embedded system: priority scheme, latency budgets, ISR design patterns, DMA integration, and shared resource protection from interrupt context.

steps.description: Inventory all interrupt sources in the system, classify them by urgency, and establish latency budgets for each.

inputs.name: peripheral-list
inputs.desc: All peripherals in the system with their interrupt capabilities

inputs.name: timing-requirements
inputs.desc: Maximum allowable latency from event to response for each interrupt source

outputs.name: interrupt-inventory
outputs.desc: Each interrupt source with: peripheral, trigger type (edge/level), frequency, required latency, and estimated ISR execution time

outputs.name: latency-budget
outputs.desc: For each interrupt: total budget breakdown into hardware latency, ISR entry overhead, processing time, and margin

process: List every interrupt source from the MCU reference manual: peripheral interrupts (UART RX, SPI complete, ADC end-of-conversion, timer overflow, GPIO edge), DMA transfer complete, fault interrupts (hard fault, bus fault, usage fault, memory management fault).

For each source, record the trigger type. Edge-triggered interrupts can be missed if the flag is not cleared before the next edge. Level-triggered interrupts keep asserting until the cause is serviced. Choose edge for pulses, level for status conditions.

Establish the latency budget for each interrupt. The total latency is: hardware stacking time + ISR entry (vector fetch, pipeline flush) + any higher-priority ISR preemption + ISR processing time. On Cortex-M, hardware stacking takes 12 cycles minimum.

Estimate ISR execution time by counting the operations needed: read status register, clear flag, transfer data (or start DMA), signal the task. Multiply instruction count by cycles-per-instruction for the target core.
Identify interrupts that can share a vector (e.g., multiple GPIO pins on the same port). Shared vectors add dispatching overhead: read the flag register to determine which pin triggered, then branch.

steps.description: Assign interrupt priority levels using the ARM NVIC model (or equivalent), configure priority grouping, and verify that nesting behavior meets latency requirements.

inputs.name: interrupt-inventory
inputs.desc: All interrupt sources with latency requirements

inputs.name: latency-budget
inputs.desc: Latency budgets per interrupt

outputs.name: priority-assignment
outputs.desc: Each interrupt with assigned preemption priority and sub-priority, plus the NVIC priority grouping configuration

outputs.name: nesting-analysis
outputs.desc: Worst-case nesting depth and the resulting stack usage on the main stack pointer (MSP)

process: Configure NVIC priority grouping. ARM Cortex-M splits the priority field into preemption priority (group) and sub-priority. More preemption bits allow more nesting levels but fewer sub-priorities. Common choice: 4 bits preemption, 0 bits sub-priority (NVIC_PriorityGroup_4) for maximum nesting control.

Assign preemption priorities: lowest number = highest urgency. Safety-critical interrupts (fault handlers, watchdog) get the highest priority. Time-critical peripheral interrupts (motor control PWM, communication frame sync) get the next tier. Bulk data transfer complete interrupts get lower priority.
Reserve priority level 0 for fault handlers that must never be blocked. The RTOS SysTick and PendSV typically get the lowest priority levels so they never delay peripheral ISRs.

Calculate worst-case nesting depth: count the maximum number of priority levels where an interrupt at each level could preempt the previous. Each nesting level adds one context frame to the MSP stack (32 bytes on Cortex-M baseline, more with FPU context).

Verify that no interrupt with a tight latency budget can be preempted by a longer-running higher-priority ISR. If so, swap priorities or split the long ISR into a short top-half and a deferred bottom-half.

steps.description: Implement ISR handlers following minimal-work design rules: hardware register access, flag clearing, data transfer, and deferred processing via RTOS notifications.

inputs.name: priority-assignment
inputs.desc: Interrupt priorities and nesting configuration

inputs.name: interrupt-inventory
inputs.desc: Each interrupt with its required actions

outputs.name: isr-implementations
outputs.desc: ISR code patterns for each interrupt type: register access sequence, flag clearing order, data movement, and RTOS notification method

outputs.name: shared-resource-protocol
outputs.desc: Rules for accessing shared data from ISR context: which mechanisms are safe (atomic operations, lock-free queues) and which are not (mutexes, malloc)

process: Follow the minimal-ISR rule: read the status register to identify the cause, clear the interrupt flag immediately (before processing for edge-triggered, after for level-triggered), move data to a buffer or queue, signal a task, return. Processing happens in the task, not the ISR.

For UART RX: read the data register (this clears the flag on most MCUs), write to a ring buffer, increment the write pointer using an atomic operation, signal the processing task via a semaphore or task notification. The ring buffer must be sized for worst-case burst at the baud rate.

For ADC end-of-conversion: read the data register, store to a DMA-like sample buffer, increment the sample counter. If the buffer is full, signal the processing task and swap to a second buffer (ping-pong pattern).

For timer overflow (periodic processing): use the ISR only to post a semaphore or set an event flag. The actual periodic work runs in a task at the appropriate priority. This keeps the ISR deterministic.

Never call functions that block or allocate memory from ISR context. Banned operations inside ISRs: mutex lock, memory allocation (malloc/new), printf/logging, queue send with a non-zero timeout. Use the 'FromISR' variants of RTOS API calls that never block.

For shared data between an ISR and a task: use atomic operations for single-word reads/writes, lock-free ring buffers for streaming data, or disable the specific interrupt briefly (not global interrupt disable) for multi-word structures.

steps.description: Integrate DMA with the interrupt architecture to offload data transfer from the CPU, reduce ISR frequency, and improve determinism.

inputs.name: isr-implementations
inputs.desc: Current ISR designs identifying data transfer bottlenecks

inputs.name: shared-resource-protocol
inputs.desc: Rules for safe data access

outputs.name: dma-configuration
outputs.desc: DMA channel assignments, transfer sizes, circular vs normal mode, and half/full transfer interrupt usage

outputs.name: revised-interrupt-load
outputs.desc: Updated interrupt frequency and CPU utilization after DMA offloading

process: Identify interrupt sources where the ISR primarily moves data: UART RX/TX byte-by-byte, SPI frame transfers, ADC multi-channel scans, memory-to-memory copies. These are candidates for DMA.

Assign DMA channels. On STM32, DMA request mapping is fixed per channel/stream. Check the reference manual for which peripheral maps to which DMA channel. Conflicts require arbitration or using a different DMA controller.

Configure DMA transfer mode: peripheral-to-memory for RX, memory-to-peripheral for TX. Set data width to match the peripheral register size. Enable circular mode for continuous ADC scanning. Use normal mode for finite-length transfers (SPI block reads).

Use half-transfer and transfer-complete interrupts for double-buffering (ping-pong). The CPU processes the first half while DMA fills the second half, and vice versa. This eliminates the latency of waiting for the full buffer.

Calculate the new interrupt rate: with DMA handling a 115200 baud UART, interrupts drop from 11,520/sec (one per byte) to roughly 23/sec (one per 512-byte DMA buffer). This frees significant CPU time.
Handle DMA error interrupts: transfer error, FIFO overrun. These indicate system problems (bus contention, misconfigured addresses). Log the error, reset the DMA channel, and resume or escalate.

steps.description: Design protection against interrupt storms that can starve task execution: rate limiting, disabling and re-enabling strategies, and watchdog-based recovery.

inputs.name: dma-configuration
inputs.desc: DMA setup reducing normal interrupt load

inputs.name: revised-interrupt-load
inputs.desc: Expected interrupt rates under normal and worst-case conditions

outputs.name: storm-protection-design
outputs.desc: Rate limiting thresholds, disable/re-enable timers, escalation actions, and watchdog integration for each interrupt source

outputs.name: interrupt-architecture-document
outputs.desc: Complete interrupt design: priority map, ISR implementations, DMA integration, storm protection, and verification checklist

process: Define the storm threshold for each interrupt: the rate above which the system cannot maintain task scheduling. For a 1 kHz tick rate, if any ISR consumes more than 50% of each tick period, tasks will miss deadlines.

Implement ISR rate monitoring: maintain a counter per interrupt source, reset every tick. If the count exceeds the threshold, disable the interrupt and start a re-enable timer. Log the event for diagnostics.

For level-triggered interrupts, a stuck peripheral can cause a storm immediately. The ISR must check if the interrupt source is still asserted after clearing. If so, disable the interrupt and flag a hardware error.

Configure the watchdog timer with a timeout shorter than the longest acceptable task starvation period. If an interrupt storm prevents the watchdog-feeding task from running, the watchdog fires and resets the system.

Document the complete interrupt architecture: a table of all interrupts with priority, ISR pattern, DMA usage, storm threshold, and the verification method (logic analyzer capture showing worst-case latency and nesting). This document is the reference for code reviews and future modifications.

description: Design a firmware bootloader: boot sequence architecture, secure boot chain with root of trust, firmware update mechanism with A/B partitioning, boot time optimization, and recovery mode.

steps.description: Design the multi-stage boot sequence from power-on reset through application entry, defining responsibilities at each stage.

inputs.name: mcu-platform
inputs.desc: MCU family, flash size, RAM size, boot ROM capabilities, and clock configuration requirements

inputs.name: security-requirements
inputs.desc: Whether secure boot is required, firmware encryption needs, and anti-rollback requirements

outputs.name: boot-stage-design
outputs.desc: Each boot stage with: entry conditions, responsibilities, memory location, size budget, and handoff mechanism

outputs.name: flash-partition-map
outputs.desc: Flash memory layout: bootloader region, application A slot, application B slot (if A/B), configuration/NVM region, factory image region

process: Define the boot stages. Stage 0: ROM bootloader (built into silicon, not modifiable). Stage 1: first-stage bootloader in protected flash (performs hardware init, validates stage 2). Stage 2: second-stage bootloader (full update logic, validates application). Stage 3: application.

The ROM bootloader (stage 0) is fixed by the silicon vendor. Understand its capabilities: which interfaces it can boot from (UART, USB, SPI), whether it checks signatures, and how it selects between boot sources (boot pins, option bytes).

Design the flash partition map. Place the bootloader at the base of flash (address 0x08000000 on STM32). Size it conservatively: 32 KB to 64 KB for most systems. The application starts at the next flash sector boundary after the bootloader. If using A/B update, split remaining flash into two equal application slots plus a configuration sector.

Define the vector table relocation mechanism. The bootloader must set VTOR (Vector Table Offset Register) to point to the application's vector table before jumping. The application's linker script must place its vector table at the slot base address.

Design the bootloader-to-application handoff: set the MSP to the value at the application's vector table base address, then branch to the reset handler address stored at vector table base + 4. Verify the MSP value is within valid RAM range before jumping (a simple integrity check).

steps.description: Implement a secure boot chain with hardware root of trust, cryptographic signature verification, and anti-rollback protection.

inputs.name: boot-stage-design
inputs.desc: Boot stages and their responsibilities

inputs.name: security-requirements
inputs.desc: Required security level, key management constraints

outputs.name: secure-boot-architecture
outputs.desc: Signature algorithm, key storage, verification flow at each stage, failure handling, and anti-rollback counter mechanism

outputs.name: key-management-plan
outputs.desc: Root key generation, signing key hierarchy, key storage (OTP fuses or secure element), and key revocation procedure

process: Select the signature algorithm. ECDSA with P-256 is the standard choice: 64-byte signature, verification in under 100 ms on a Cortex-M4 at 168 MHz. RSA-2048 is an alternative but signatures are 256 bytes and verification is slower without hardware acceleration.

Store the root public key in one-time-programmable (OTP) fuses or a secure element. This is the hardware root of trust. The ROM bootloader or first-stage bootloader uses this key to verify the next stage. Once burned, the key cannot be changed, so key generation must follow a ceremony with offline storage of the private key.

Implement the chain of trust: ROM verifies stage 1 using the OTP root key. Stage 1 verifies stage 2 using a key embedded in stage 1 (or the same root key). Stage 2 verifies the application. Each stage only executes the next if verification passes.

Add a firmware image header before each signed blob: magic number, version number, image size, hardware compatibility ID, signature. The verifier reads the header, hashes the image (SHA-256), then checks the signature against the hash.

Implement anti-rollback: store a monotonic counter in OTP fuses or a protected NVM region. Each firmware image header contains a minimum-version field. The bootloader refuses to boot any image with a version lower than the stored counter. After successful boot, update the counter to the running version.

steps.description: Design the firmware update mechanism: A/B partitioning for atomic updates, differential updates for bandwidth-constrained links, and update state machine.

inputs.name: flash-partition-map
inputs.desc: Flash layout with bootloader, app slots, and config regions

inputs.name: secure-boot-architecture
inputs.desc: Signature verification flow that the update must integrate with

outputs.name: update-state-machine
outputs.desc: States: idle, downloading, verifying, committing, rolling-back. Transitions and persistent flags for each state.

outputs.name: update-protocol
outputs.desc: Transport protocol (UART/USB/BLE/cellular), chunk size, error handling, resume capability, and total update time estimate

process: Choose the update strategy. A/B partitioning: the running application writes the new image to the inactive slot, the bootloader validates and swaps on next boot. This is atomic (power loss at any point is safe) but requires 2x the flash for application code.

If flash is too small for A/B, use in-place update with a recovery image: the bootloader copies the new image over the running application, with a factory recovery image in a protected region. This is not atomic, but the recovery image handles interrupted updates.

Design the update state machine with persistent flags stored in a dedicated flash sector (or the last page of each slot). States: IDLE (boot normally), DOWNLOAD_IN_PROGRESS (resume if interrupted), VERIFY_PENDING (new image received, needs validation), BOOT_NEW (bootloader should try the new slot), CONFIRMED (new image booted and confirmed by application), ROLLBACK (new image failed, revert to previous).

For bandwidth-constrained links (BLE, LoRa), implement delta updates: generate a binary diff (bsdiff or similar) between old and new firmware. The device applies the patch to produce the new image. This reduces transfer size by 60% to 90% for typical firmware changes but requires RAM for the patching algorithm.

Handle power loss at every transition. The golden rule: never erase the current working image until the new image is fully written and verified. With A/B, this is automatic. With in-place update, copy the current image to backup before erasing.

The application must confirm the new firmware within a timeout (e.g., 3 successful boot cycles or an explicit confirm command). If confirmation does not arrive, the bootloader rolls back to the previous version on the next reset.

steps.description: Reduce boot time from power-on to application ready through clock configuration optimization, lazy initialization, and parallel init sequencing.

inputs.name: update-state-machine
inputs.desc: Update mechanism design that affects boot path decisions

inputs.name: boot-stage-design
inputs.desc: Current boot stages and their execution times

outputs.name: boot-time-breakdown
outputs.desc: Time in ms for each boot phase: oscillator startup, PLL lock, flash init, signature verification, peripheral init, application init

outputs.name: optimization-actions
outputs.desc: Specific changes to reduce boot time with measured before/after for each

process: Measure the current boot time with a GPIO pin toggled at each stage boundary. Use an oscilloscope to capture the full boot sequence. Common breakdown: oscillator startup (1 to 10 ms), PLL lock (0.5 to 2 ms), bootloader execution (5 to 50 ms), signature verification (10 to 200 ms), application init (varies).

Optimize oscillator startup: if using an external crystal, the startup time depends on load capacitance and crystal parameters. Reduce load caps to the minimum recommended by the crystal manufacturer. Or start on the internal RC oscillator and switch to the crystal after PLL lock.

For secure boot, pre-compute partial hashes. If the firmware image has not changed since last boot (stored hash matches), skip the full verification and use a fast integrity check (CRC32 of key sections) instead. Full verification runs only after an update.

Use lazy initialization: only init peripherals that are needed immediately. Defer initialization of communication interfaces, sensors, and displays until the first access. This moves time from the boot path to the first use of each peripheral.

Parallelize initialization where hardware allows: start ADC calibration while configuring communication peripherals. Start DMA-based sensor reads while the display is initializing. Track dependencies to avoid initializing a peripheral before its clock and GPIO are ready.

Measure the optimized boot time and record the improvements. The target depends on the application: consumer devices need sub-1-second boot, industrial controllers can tolerate 2 to 5 seconds, automotive ECUs have strict sub-100-ms requirements for some functions.

steps.description: Design the recovery mode: entry conditions, fail-safe communication interface, factory reset capability, and brick prevention.

inputs.name: boot-time-breakdown
inputs.desc: Boot timing analysis showing where failures can occur

inputs.name: optimization-actions
inputs.desc: Optimized boot path that recovery must be independent of

outputs.name: recovery-design
outputs.desc: Recovery entry conditions (button hold, magic byte, boot failure counter), recovery communication interface, and factory reset procedure

outputs.name: bootloader-design-document
outputs.desc: Complete bootloader specification: boot stages, secure boot, update mechanism, boot time budget, recovery mode, and test plan

process: Define recovery entry conditions. Primary: hardware button held during reset (check GPIO state in bootloader before jumping to app). Secondary: boot failure counter (increment on each boot attempt, clear on successful app confirmation; enter recovery after 3 consecutive failures). Tertiary: magic value written to a specific RAM address that survives reset (warm reset recovery trigger).

The recovery communication interface must be independent of the application firmware. Use the ROM bootloader's built-in UART/USB bootloader if available, or implement a minimal protocol in the first-stage bootloader. This interface must work even if the application and second-stage bootloader are both corrupted.

Implement factory reset: erase the application slots and configuration, then load the factory image from a write-protected flash region. The factory image must be old enough to be stable but new enough to include the update mechanism for field upgrades.

Prevent bricking by design. The first-stage bootloader must be in write-protected flash (use option bytes or flash protection bits). It must be small enough to be thoroughly tested and rarely updated. If it must be updated, the ROM bootloader serves as the last-resort recovery.

Document the complete bootloader design: flash map, boot sequence with timing, secure boot chain, update state machine, recovery procedures, and a test matrix covering every state transition including power loss at each step.

description: Design the memory architecture for an embedded system: memory map, linker script configuration, stack and heap sizing from call graph analysis, MPU configuration, DMA buffer placement, and deterministic memory allocation.

steps.description: Design the system memory map by assigning flash and RAM regions to bootloader, application, data, and peripheral access, based on MCU memory architecture.

inputs.name: mcu-memory-spec
inputs.desc: MCU memory regions (flash base/size, SRAM banks, CCM RAM if present, backup SRAM, peripheral base), and any memory-mapped external memories

inputs.name: application-requirements
inputs.desc: Code size estimate, static data size, dynamic memory needs, DMA requirements, and any special memory needs (tightly-coupled, non-cacheable)

outputs.name: memory-map
outputs.desc: Each memory region with: base address, size, contents (code, rodata, data, bss, heap, stacks, DMA buffers, config/NVM), and access attributes (read/write/execute, cacheable, shareable)

outputs.name: region-allocation-table
outputs.desc: Detailed allocation within each region: section names, sizes, alignment requirements, and growth direction

process: Start from the MCU memory map in the reference manual. ARM Cortex-M defines: 0x00000000 to 0x1FFFFFFF for code (flash maps here), 0x20000000 to 0x3FFFFFFF for SRAM, 0x40000000 to 0x5FFFFFFF for peripherals, 0xE0000000 for system control (NVIC, SysTick, debug).

Partition flash: bootloader at base, application code after bootloader end (sector-aligned), read-only data (const, strings, lookup tables) adjacent to code, configuration/calibration data in the last flash sector(s) for independent erase.

Partition SRAM: .data and .bss at SRAM base, stacks growing downward from a defined boundary, heap growing upward from .bss end (if heap is used), DMA buffers at specific addresses required by DMA controller alignment. On STM32 with multiple SRAM banks, place DMA buffers in SRAM1/SRAM2 accessible by the DMA controller.

If the MCU has CCM (core-coupled memory), use it for stack and frequently accessed variables because it has zero-wait-state access. CCM is not DMA-accessible on most STM32, so DMA buffers must go in main SRAM.

For systems with data cache (Cortex-M7), mark DMA buffer regions as non-cacheable to prevent coherence issues. Alternatively, use cache maintenance operations (clean/invalidate) around DMA transfers, but the non-cacheable approach is simpler and less error-prone.

steps.description: Write the linker script (GNU LD or equivalent) that implements the memory map, placing each section in the correct region with proper alignment and initialization.

inputs.name: memory-map
inputs.desc: Memory regions with contents and attributes

inputs.name: region-allocation-table
inputs.desc: Section assignments and alignment requirements

outputs.name: linker-script
outputs.desc: Complete linker script with MEMORY definitions, SECTIONS placements, symbol definitions for startup code (.data copy, .bss zero, stack pointer), and alignment directives

outputs.name: startup-requirements
outputs.desc: What the startup code must do based on the linker script: copy .data from flash to RAM, zero .bss, set MSP, call constructors, branch to main

process: Define the MEMORY block: each physical memory region with origin and length. Name them clearly: FLASH, SRAM, CCM, BACKUP_SRAM. The origin and length must match the MCU datasheet exactly.

Define the SECTIONS block. Place .isr_vector first in FLASH (the vector table must be at the flash base for the default VTOR). Follow with .text (code), .rodata (constants), .ARM.extab and .ARM.exidx (exception handling tables if C++ is used).

The .data section is loaded in FLASH but runs from RAM. Use the AT> directive: '.data : { *(.data*) } > SRAM AT> FLASH'. Define _sidata (load address in flash), _sdata (start in RAM), _edata (end in RAM) symbols for the startup code to copy.
The .bss section is zero-initialized and lives only in RAM. Define _sbss and _ebss symbols. The startup code zeroes this region before calling main.

Place the stack at the top of SRAM (or CCM) with a defined size symbol. The first word of the vector table is the initial MSP value, which the linker script provides: _estack = ORIGIN(SRAM) + LENGTH(SRAM). Alternatively, reserve a fixed-size stack section.

Add ASSERT statements to catch overflows at link time: ASSERT((_edata - _sdata) + (_ebss - _sbss) + _Min_Heap_Size + _Min_Stack_Size <= LENGTH(SRAM), 'RAM overflow'). This prevents silent memory corruption from a build that compiles but does not fit.

steps.description: Determine stack and heap sizes using static call graph analysis, compiler-generated stack usage data, and runtime verification.

inputs.name: linker-script
inputs.desc: Current linker script with stack and heap size symbols

inputs.name: startup-requirements
inputs.desc: Startup code requirements affecting initial stack usage

outputs.name: stack-size-calculation
outputs.desc: Per-task stack requirement with breakdown: deepest call path, local variable sum, interrupt preemption overhead, FPU context, and safety margin

outputs.name: heap-elimination-plan
outputs.desc: Strategy to eliminate or minimize heap usage through static allocation, memory pools, and stack-allocated buffers

process: Compile with -fstack-usage (GCC) to generate .su files showing stack usage per function. Parse these to find the function with the deepest total stack path: sum from main() (or task entry) through the deepest call chain.

Account for call-stack overhead: each function call pushes the return address (4 bytes on ARM) plus any callee-saved registers the function uses (up to 32 bytes for all callee-saved regs). The -fstack-usage output includes this.

Add interrupt preemption overhead: on Cortex-M, an interrupt pushes 8 registers (32 bytes) automatically. With FPU in use and lazy stacking enabled, an additional 72 bytes are reserved (but only used if the ISR uses floating point). If RTOS is used, the ISR stack is separate (MSP), so this adds to the ISR stack, not the task stack.

For heap: the safest approach in embedded systems is to eliminate it. Replace malloc with static buffers sized at compile time, memory pools for fixed-size allocations, and stack-allocated arrays for temporary buffers. If heap is unavoidable, define the minimum heap size as the peak concurrent allocation measured during testing.

Verify at runtime: fill the stack region with a canary pattern (0xDEADBEEF) at startup. Periodically check the canary from the bottom up. The first non-canary byte is the high-water mark. The margin between high-water mark and stack bottom should be at least 15% of the total stack.
Record the final sizes in the linker script as _Min_Stack_Size and _Min_Heap_Size. These symbols are used by the ASSERT to catch RAM overflow at link time.

steps.description: Configure the Memory Protection Unit to enforce access permissions, prevent stack overflow corruption, and isolate DMA buffers from application code.

inputs.name: stack-size-calculation
inputs.desc: Stack sizes and locations for MPU guard regions

inputs.name: memory-map
inputs.desc: Memory regions with required access attributes

outputs.name: mpu-region-table
outputs.desc: Each MPU region with: base address, size, access permissions (privileged/unprivileged, read/write/execute), memory attributes (cacheable, bufferable, shareable), and sub-region disable mask

outputs.name: fault-handler-design
outputs.desc: Memory management fault handler that reports the faulting address, access type, and which MPU rule was violated

process: ARM Cortex-M MPU has 8 or 16 regions (check the core revision). Each region must be a power-of-2 size, naturally aligned. Plan regions from most to least restrictive, using region priority (higher-numbered regions override lower).

Region 0: full flash as read-only, execute-allowed. This is the default background for code. Region 1: RAM as read-write, no-execute. This prevents code execution from RAM (a basic exploit mitigation).

Place a guard region (no access) at the bottom of each task stack. Size it to one MPU minimum region size (32 bytes on ARMv7-M, 256 bytes practical minimum due to alignment). A stack overflow triggers a MemManage fault instead of silently corrupting adjacent memory.

Mark DMA buffer regions as non-cacheable and shareable. On Cortex-M7 with cache, this is critical: TEX=001, C=0, B=1 (device shareable) or TEX=000, C=0, B=0 (strongly ordered). Without this, cached writes may not reach the DMA controller.

If running with unprivileged tasks (RTOS with MPU integration), configure per-task MPU regions to limit each task's access to only its own stack and designated shared regions. The RTOS context switch reconfigures the MPU for each task.

Implement the MemManage fault handler to capture MMFAR (faulting address), MMFSR (fault status), and the stacked PC (the instruction that caused the fault). Log these values and trigger a controlled error response.

steps.description: Design and implement a deterministic memory allocation scheme using memory pools and block allocators, eliminating heap fragmentation and non-deterministic allocation times.

inputs.name: mpu-region-table
inputs.desc: MPU configuration constraining where allocations can live

inputs.name: heap-elimination-plan
inputs.desc: Strategy for replacing heap with fixed allocators

outputs.name: allocator-design
outputs.desc: Memory pool definitions (block size, count, location), allocation API, deallocation API, and overflow handling

outputs.name: memory-architecture-document
outputs.desc: Complete memory design: map, linker script, stack/heap analysis, MPU config, allocators, and verification methodology

process: Profile the application's dynamic memory usage. Log every allocation and deallocation with size and caller. Group allocations into size classes. Typical embedded patterns: many small allocations (16 to 64 bytes for protocol buffers) and a few large ones (512 to 4096 bytes for data buffers).

Create a memory pool for each size class. A pool is a static array of fixed-size blocks with a free list (singly-linked list through the blocks themselves, zero overhead when a block is free). Allocation is O(1): pop from free list. Deallocation is O(1): push to free list.
Size each pool based on worst-case concurrent usage measured during profiling, plus 20% margin. Compile-time ASSERT that the total pool sizes fit in the allocated RAM region.

For allocations that do not fit any pool, use a static scratch buffer with a bump allocator (allocate by advancing a pointer, free by resetting the pointer). This works for request-scoped allocations where everything is freed at once.

Make all allocation failures visible and handled. No allocator should return NULL silently. Options: assert (catch in testing), error code (caller handles), or pre-verified design (prove at design time that the pool cannot be exhausted because usage is bounded).

Document the complete memory architecture: physical memory map, linker script with ASSERT guards, per-task stack sizes with analysis, MPU region table, memory pool specifications, and the verification approach (static analysis of allocation paths, runtime canary checks, profiling under stress test).

description: Design power management for an embedded system: sleep mode selection, wake source configuration, DVFS, peripheral clock gating, current profiling, and battery life estimation from duty cycle analysis.

steps.description: Establish the power budget by profiling current consumption in each operating mode and calculating the required battery life against available energy.

inputs.name: system-spec
inputs.desc: MCU, peripherals, sensors, communication modules, and their operating voltages and current consumption from datasheets

inputs.name: battery-spec
inputs.desc: Battery chemistry, nominal voltage, capacity in mAh, self-discharge rate, and operating temperature range

outputs.name: power-profile
outputs.desc: Current consumption in each mode: active-full, active-reduced, sleep, deep-sleep, and standby, measured at the system level including regulator efficiency losses

outputs.name: power-budget-gap
outputs.desc: Required battery life vs calculated battery life. If a gap exists, the target current reduction needed to close it.

process: Measure baseline current: board powered from a bench supply through a current sense resistor (10 to 100 mOhm depending on current range) or a dedicated power profiler (Nordic PPK2 or similar). Measure at the battery input, not after the regulator, to capture regulator quiescent current and efficiency losses.

Profile each operating mode separately: CPU running at full clock with all peripherals active, CPU running with unused peripherals disabled, sleep mode (CPU halted, peripherals running), deep sleep (CPU and most peripherals halted, only wake sources active), standby/shutdown (only RTC and wake pin active).

Calculate battery life: Life_hours = Battery_mAh / Average_current_mA. For duty-cycled operation: Average_mA = (active_mA * active_time + sleep_mA * sleep_time) / total_cycle_time. Include battery self-discharge (typically 2% to 5% per month for lithium).

Account for regulator efficiency. A switching regulator at 85% efficiency delivering 3.3V from a 3.7V LiPo means the battery-side current is 3.3/3.7 * load_current / 0.85. An LDO is simpler: battery current equals load current, but the voltage drop is wasted as heat.
Identify the power budget gap: if required lifetime exceeds calculated lifetime, compute the average current reduction needed. This sets the target for the optimization steps.

steps.description: Select and configure the optimal sleep mode for each system state, mapping wake sources to system events and designing the sleep/wake state machine.

inputs.name: power-profile
inputs.desc: Current in each mode

inputs.name: power-budget-gap
inputs.desc: Required current reduction

outputs.name: sleep-mode-selection
outputs.desc: For each system state: which MCU sleep mode, which peripherals remain active, which clocks run, and expected current draw

outputs.name: wake-source-map
outputs.desc: Each wake source (RTC alarm, GPIO pin, UART activity, comparator, I2C address match) with its latency from trigger to application code running

process: Map the MCU's sleep modes to current consumption from the datasheet. Typical ARM Cortex-M hierarchy: Sleep (WFI, CPU stopped, peripherals run: 1 to 10 mA), Stop (most clocks off, SRAM retained, wake from EXTI: 1 to 100 uA), Standby (only backup domain, wake from RTC/WKUP pin: 1 to 5 uA), Shutdown (everything off: under 100 nA).

For each system state (monitoring, communicating, processing, idle), select the deepest sleep mode that preserves the required peripheral operation and meets the wake latency requirement. Deeper modes save more power but take longer to wake: Sleep wakes in cycles, Stop in 2 to 10 us, Standby requires full boot.

Configure wake sources. RTC alarm for periodic wake (sensor sampling). GPIO EXTI for external events (button press, sensor interrupt). UART activity detection for incoming commands (USART wake from Stop on start bit). I2C address match for bus wakeup in multi-device systems.

Design the sleep/wake state machine. Track the current state and what events can occur. Before entering sleep: ensure all pending operations are complete (DMA transfers done, UART TX buffer flushed, flash writes committed). After wake: identify the wake source (check wake flags), reinitialize only what was lost in the sleep mode (clock tree for Stop, full init for Standby).

Handle the idle task in an RTOS: the idle task should enter the deepest allowed sleep mode. The RTOS tick must wake the system before the next scheduled task. Tickless idle mode (available in FreeRTOS, Zephyr) suppresses the tick during long idle periods, allowing the system to stay in deep sleep.

steps.description: Minimize active-mode power by disabling clocks to unused peripherals, reducing clock frequencies where full speed is not needed, and power-gating entire domains.

inputs.name: sleep-mode-selection
inputs.desc: Sleep modes and which peripherals must remain active

inputs.name: wake-source-map
inputs.desc: Wake sources requiring specific clocks or peripherals

outputs.name: clock-gating-table
outputs.desc: Each peripheral clock with: enabled/disabled per system state, clock source, frequency, and the current savings from disabling

outputs.name: dvfs-configuration
outputs.desc: Voltage and frequency scaling levels: clock frequency, core voltage, flash wait states, and current consumption for each level

process: Audit every peripheral clock enable bit. On STM32, the RCC_AHBxENR and RCC_APBxENR registers control peripheral clocks. Most are disabled by reset but driver initialization enables them. Disable after use: turn off the ADC clock after conversion complete, turn off SPI clock after the transfer.

For peripherals used intermittently, enable the clock just before the operation and disable immediately after. The clock enable propagation delay is typically 1 to 2 bus clock cycles. Do not forget to disable the clock in error paths.

Implement dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS). Define 2 to 4 operating points: full speed for computation, medium speed for communication, low speed for housekeeping. Each operating point specifies: CPU clock, bus clocks (AHB/APB), core voltage (if adjustable via internal regulator), and flash wait states.

When scaling down frequency, adjust flash wait states first (increase them), then reduce the clock. When scaling up, increase the clock first, then reduce wait states. Getting this order wrong causes the CPU to read garbage from flash.

Measure the current at each operating point with the actual workload, not just idle. A 48 MHz Cortex-M at 30% utilization may draw less average current than a 16 MHz Cortex-M at 90% utilization because the faster CPU finishes and sleeps sooner (race to sleep).

steps.description: Profile the system's current consumption over time with sub-millisecond resolution to identify power spikes, inefficient duty cycles, and optimization opportunities.

inputs.name: clock-gating-table
inputs.desc: Peripheral clock states per system mode

inputs.name: dvfs-configuration
inputs.desc: Frequency/voltage operating points

outputs.name: current-waveform
outputs.desc: Time-resolved current profile at sub-ms resolution showing each operational phase with annotated events (wake, transmit, sleep entry)

outputs.name: optimization-targets
outputs.desc: Ranked list of power reduction opportunities with estimated mAh savings per day for each

process: Set up a power profiler that captures current with at least 1 us resolution and a dynamic range from 100 nA to 100 mA. The Nordic Power Profiler Kit 2 or Joulescope JS220 are suitable. Connect in series between the battery/supply and the board's power input.

Run a representative duty cycle: the system should go through all operational states including communication, sensing, processing, and sleeping. Capture a long enough trace to include several complete cycles.

Annotate the current waveform with GPIO debug signals: toggle a pin at each state transition so the power trace correlates with firmware events. This shows exactly which code section causes each current spike or plateau.

Identify power waste: time spent in active mode after the work is complete (waiting for an event instead of sleeping), peripherals left enabled during sleep (a common bug), radio transmit at higher power than needed, or excessive wake-up frequency.

Rank the optimization opportunities by impact: mAh_saved_per_day = (current_reduction_mA * duration_per_cycle_ms * cycles_per_day) / 3600000. Focus on the largest contributors first. A 1 mA reduction during a 10 ms active phase that runs 1000 times per day saves only 0.003 mAh. A 10 uA reduction during a 59-second sleep that repeats 1440 times per day saves 0.14 mAh.

steps.description: Compute the final battery life estimate from measured current profiles, incorporating temperature effects, aging, and manufacturing variation.

inputs.name: current-waveform
inputs.desc: Time-resolved current measurements

inputs.name: optimization-targets
inputs.desc: Planned optimizations with expected savings

outputs.name: battery-life-estimate
outputs.desc: Expected battery life in days under nominal, best-case, and worst-case conditions, with the assumptions behind each

outputs.name: power-management-document
outputs.desc: Complete power design: modes, wake sources, clock gating, DVFS, measured profiles, battery life calculation, and design margins

process: Calculate average current from the measured profile: integrate the current over one complete duty cycle and divide by the cycle duration. For complex profiles with variable cycle times, use the per-day energy consumption in mWh.

Apply temperature derating: battery capacity decreases at cold temperatures. A typical LiPo delivers 80% of rated capacity at 0 degrees C and 60% at -20 degrees C. Use the battery manufacturer's temperature-capacity curve for the expected operating range.

Apply aging derating: lithium cells lose capacity over charge cycles. After 500 cycles, expect 80% of initial capacity. If the product's required lifetime includes many charge cycles, use the end-of-life capacity, not the fresh-battery capacity.

Apply manufacturing variation: add 10% to the average current to account for component tolerance (regulator quiescent current, leakage through GPIO pins, crystal oscillator current). Use worst-case datasheet values, not typical.

Compute three estimates: best-case (nominal current, rated capacity, room temperature), nominal (measured average current + 10% margin, rated capacity derated for mid-life aging), worst-case (max current, min capacity at coldest operating temperature, end-of-life). The worst-case must meet the product requirement. Document all assumptions.

description: Implement embedded communication protocols from hardware configuration through driver design: SPI, I2C, UART, CAN, USB, and Ethernet MAC/PHY interfaces with proper timing, error handling, and DMA integration.

steps.description: Implement SPI master and slave with proper clock polarity/phase configuration, chip select management, DMA for bulk transfers, and multi-slave bus topology.

inputs.name: spi-device-specs
inputs.desc: Datasheets for all SPI devices on the bus: supported modes (CPOL/CPHA), maximum clock frequency, timing diagrams, and frame format

inputs.name: throughput-requirements
inputs.desc: Required data transfer rates and maximum latency for each SPI device

outputs.name: spi-configuration
outputs.desc: SPI peripheral config: mode (0/1/2/3), clock divider, frame size, MSB/LSB first, NSS management, and DMA channel assignments

outputs.name: spi-driver-api
outputs.desc: Driver interface: init, transfer (full-duplex), send (half-duplex TX), receive (half-duplex RX), transfer-DMA, chip-select control, and error handling

process: Determine SPI mode from the slave device datasheet. Mode 0 (CPOL=0, CPHA=0): clock idle low, sample on rising edge. Mode 3 (CPOL=1, CPHA=1): clock idle high, sample on falling edge. Modes 0 and 3 are most common. Match the master configuration to what each slave requires.

Set the clock divider to produce a frequency at or below the slave's maximum SPI clock. The MCU SPI peripheral divides the bus clock by powers of 2 (2, 4, 8, ... 256). Choose the highest frequency that stays within spec. Account for signal integrity: long traces or high capacitance may require a slower clock even if the slave supports faster.

Manage chip select (CS) in software (GPIO) for flexibility: assert CS (drive low) before the transfer, deassert (drive high) after. Some devices require CS to stay asserted between command and data bytes. Hardware NSS management does not support this pattern on most MCUs.

For transfers larger than a few bytes, use DMA: configure TX DMA to feed the SPI TX register and RX DMA to drain the SPI RX register simultaneously. For TX-only (display writes), configure RX DMA to a dummy location or disable it. The DMA complete interrupt signals the end of transfer.

For multi-slave buses, ensure each slave's CS is deasserted when not selected. If slaves have different SPI modes, reconfigure the SPI peripheral before each slave transaction. The reconfiguration must happen while the SPI is disabled to avoid glitches.

steps.description: Implement I2C with proper bus configuration, clock stretching handling, multi-master arbitration, and error recovery for stuck buses.

inputs.name: i2c-device-list
inputs.desc: All I2C devices with addresses, speed grade (standard 100 kHz, fast 400 kHz, fast-plus 1 MHz), and any quirks from datasheets

inputs.name: bus-topology
inputs.desc: Wire length, pull-up resistor values, number of devices, and total bus capacitance

outputs.name: i2c-configuration
outputs.desc: I2C timing parameters (SCL frequency, rise time, fall time, setup/hold times), pull-up resistor selection, and analog/digital filter settings

outputs.name: i2c-driver-api
outputs.desc: Driver interface: init, write-register, read-register, write-block, read-block, bus-recovery, and address-scan

process: Select pull-up resistor values. The minimum value is set by the I2C output sink current (IOL = 3 mA for standard mode) and VDD: R_min = VDD / IOL. The maximum is set by the rise time requirement and bus capacitance: R_max = t_rise / (0.8473 * C_bus). For 400 kHz with 200 pF bus capacitance and 3.3V, typical values are 2.2 kOhm to 4.7 kOhm.

Configure the I2C timing registers. Modern MCUs (STM32 I2C v2) have a timing register calculated from the input clock, desired SCL frequency, and signal timing. Use the vendor's I2C timing calculation tool or the reference manual formula. Verify with an oscilloscope that SCL frequency, setup time, and hold time meet I2C spec.

Handle clock stretching: the slave holds SCL low to pause the master. The I2C peripheral handles this in hardware, but set a timeout to detect a stuck slave. If SCL is held low beyond the timeout, trigger bus recovery.

Implement bus recovery: if SDA is stuck low (slave holding it during an interrupted transfer), toggle SCL up to 9 times as a master to clock out the stuck slave, then issue a STOP condition. This is defined in the I2C specification and recovers most stuck-bus conditions.

For multi-master systems, implement arbitration-lost handling: when the peripheral detects arbitration loss (another master won), abort the current transfer and retry after a random back-off. The I2C hardware handles the bit-level arbitration; the driver handles the retry logic.

steps.description: Implement CAN bus communication with proper bit timing calculation from oscillator tolerance and bus length, message filtering, and bus-off recovery.

inputs.name: can-network-spec
inputs.desc: Bus speed (125k/250k/500k/1M), bus length, number of nodes, transceiver type, and termination

inputs.name: message-definitions
inputs.desc: CAN message IDs, DLCs, signal definitions, and cycle times for each message

outputs.name: can-bit-timing
outputs.desc: Bit timing parameters: prescaler, time segment 1, time segment 2, SJW, sample point percentage, and oscillator tolerance analysis

outputs.name: can-driver-api
outputs.desc: Driver interface: init, send-message, receive-callback, filter-config, bus-status, error-counters, and bus-off recovery

process: Calculate bit timing parameters. The CAN bit is divided into: sync segment (1 TQ), propagation segment, phase segment 1, and phase segment 2. Total TQ per bit = prescaler * peripheral_clock / bitrate. The sample point (typically 75% to 87.5% of the bit time) is set by the ratio of (sync + prop + phase1) to total TQ.

Account for oscillator tolerance. CAN requires all nodes to sample within the correct bit. The maximum oscillator frequency deviation depends on the SJW (synchronization jump width) setting: df_max = min(SJW / (2 * 10 * bit_time_in_TQ), SJW / (20 * bit_time_in_TQ)). For 500 kbps with 16 TQ/bit and SJW=1, this allows 0.3% tolerance. A 20 ppm crystal easily meets this; a ceramic resonator at 0.5% does not.

Account for propagation delay from bus length: propagation_delay = 2 * (bus_length_m * 5 ns/m + transceiver_delay). The propagation segment must be at least this value in TQ. For a 40-meter bus with 150 ns transceiver delay: (2 * (40*5 + 150)) = 700 ns.

Configure hardware message filters. Most CAN controllers support ID masking (accept messages where ID AND mask equals filter AND mask) and ID list mode (accept only specific IDs). Use masks for ranges (e.g., accept all messages from a node) and lists for individual high-priority messages. Unfiltered messages waste CPU time in the receive interrupt.

Implement bus-off recovery. CAN controllers enter bus-off state after 256 error events (transmit error counter reaches 256). Recovery options: automatic recovery after 128 sequences of 11 recessive bits (ISO 11898 specified), or manual recovery triggered by the application after a delay. Always log bus-off events for diagnostics.

steps.description: Implement UART communication with proper framing, baud rate configuration, DMA-based reception for continuous data streams, and protocol layer design.

inputs.name: uart-requirements
inputs.desc: Baud rate, data bits, parity, stop bits, flow control (hardware RTS/CTS or software XON/XOFF), and the higher-level protocol carried over UART

inputs.name: data-patterns
inputs.desc: Expected message sizes, frequency, burst patterns, and required response latency

outputs.name: uart-configuration
outputs.desc: UART peripheral settings, baud rate error analysis, DMA configuration for RX/TX, and idle line detection setup

outputs.name: framing-protocol
outputs.desc: Message framing design: start delimiter, length field, payload, CRC, and end delimiter with timeout-based frame sync recovery

process: Calculate baud rate generator settings. The baud rate divisor = peripheral_clock / (oversampling * baud_rate). Common oversampling is 16x (standard) or 8x (for higher baud rates on slower clocks). The actual baud rate will differ from the target by the rounding error in the divisor. Keep this error under 2% for reliable communication; under 1% for long frames.

For continuous reception, use DMA in circular mode writing to a ring buffer. Enable idle line detection interrupt: the UART signals when the line is idle for one frame duration after receiving data. This interrupt fires at the end of each packet, telling the application how much data arrived without polling.

Alternative for framed protocols: use DMA in normal mode with a timeout. Start DMA for the expected message length. If the full message does not arrive within the timeout, process the partial data and resync. This handles variable-length messages and noise on the line.

Design the framing protocol for noisy or multi-message environments. A reliable frame: sync byte(s) (e.g., 0xAA 0x55), length field, sequence number, payload, CRC-16. The sync bytes allow the receiver to find frame boundaries after a line error. The CRC catches corrupted frames. The sequence number detects dropped messages.

Implement frame synchronization recovery: if a received frame fails CRC, scan the receive buffer byte-by-byte for the next sync sequence. Discard everything before it and attempt to parse a new frame from the sync. This recovers from any single burst error without resetting the connection.

steps.description: Implement a USB device with proper descriptor hierarchy, endpoint configuration, enumeration handling, and class-specific protocol for CDC, HID, or custom bulk.

inputs.name: usb-class-requirements
inputs.desc: Required USB class (CDC/ACM for virtual COM port, HID for input devices, mass storage, custom bulk), transfer types needed, and data rates

inputs.name: framing-protocol
inputs.desc: Application protocol that will run over USB if applicable

outputs.name: descriptor-hierarchy
outputs.desc: Device descriptor, configuration descriptor, interface descriptors, endpoint descriptors, and string descriptors with all fields specified

outputs.name: usb-driver-api
outputs.desc: Driver interface: init, connect, disconnect, send-data, receive-callback, suspend/resume handling, and class-specific requests

process: Build the descriptor hierarchy from bottom up. Endpoint descriptors define the pipes: direction (IN/OUT), transfer type (control/bulk/interrupt/isochronous), max packet size (64 bytes for full-speed bulk, 512 for high-speed), and polling interval (for interrupt endpoints). Interface descriptors group endpoints into a function. Configuration descriptor wraps interfaces.

For CDC/ACM (virtual COM port): two interfaces. Interface 0 (CDC control): one interrupt IN endpoint for serial state notifications. Interface 1 (CDC data): one bulk IN and one bulk OUT endpoint for data. Include the CDC functional descriptors (header, call management, ACM, union) between the interface and endpoint descriptors.

Implement the enumeration state machine. On USB reset: configure endpoint 0 for control transfers (64-byte max packet). Handle standard requests: GET_DESCRIPTOR (return device, config, string descriptors), SET_ADDRESS (move from default to addressed state), SET_CONFIGURATION (move to configured state, enable data endpoints). Handle class-specific requests: SET_LINE_CODING and SET_CONTROL_LINE_STATE for CDC.

Handle USB suspend and resume for power management. The host signals suspend by stopping SOF packets for 3 ms. The device must reduce current to under 2.5 mA (for bus-powered devices). On resume (bus activity detected), restore full operation. Implement remote wakeup if the application needs to wake the host.

For data transfer, use double-buffered endpoints: the USB hardware fills one buffer while the application processes the other. This prevents gaps in continuous data transfer. The bulk transfer protocol handles flow control: the host will not send another OUT packet until the device ACKs (NAK if busy), and the device will not send IN data until the host polls.

description: Design watchdog and runtime safety mechanisms for embedded systems: watchdog selection and configuration, multi-task monitoring, safety-critical challenge-response, and runtime self-tests for IEC 61508 and ISO 26262 compliance.

steps.description: Select between independent and windowed watchdog, calculate the timeout from worst-case execution paths, and configure the reload strategy.

inputs.name: system-timing
inputs.desc: Worst-case task execution times, interrupt latencies, and the maximum acceptable time from fault to system response

inputs.name: safety-requirements
inputs.desc: Target safety integrity level (SIL 1-4 or ASIL A-D), required diagnostic coverage, and safe state definition

outputs.name: watchdog-config
outputs.desc: Watchdog type (independent/windowed/external), timeout value, window bounds (for windowed), clock source, and reload point in code

outputs.name: fault-detection-time
outputs.desc: Maximum time from software fault to watchdog reset, including worst-case feed-just-before-fault scenario

process: Choose watchdog type. Independent watchdog (IWDG on STM32): simple timeout, clocked from a separate low-speed oscillator (independent of system clock failures). Windowed watchdog (WWDG): must be fed within a specific window (not too early, not too late), detects both stuck and timing faults. External watchdog IC: highest integrity, completely independent of the MCU.

Calculate the timeout. The watchdog timeout must be: longer than the worst-case task cycle (so normal operation never triggers it) but shorter than the maximum time to reach the safe state after a fault. Typical rule: timeout = 2x to 3x the longest normal task cycle. For a 100 ms main loop, a 200 ms to 300 ms timeout.

For windowed watchdog, set the early boundary to reject feeds that come too quickly (indicating a task is spinning without doing its work) and the late boundary to catch tasks that are stuck. Window = [earliest_normal_feed + margin, timeout - margin].

The worst-case fault detection time equals the timeout period: a fault could occur immediately after a successful watchdog feed. To reduce this, feed the watchdog more frequently and only from the correct execution path (not from a simple timer interrupt, which would still run even if the application is stuck).

For SIL 3 or ASIL C/D, an external watchdog IC with Q&A (question-and-answer) capability is required. The MCU must compute a correct response to the watchdog's challenge within the timeout. A stuck MCU cannot produce correct answers. This achieves higher diagnostic coverage than an internal watchdog alone.

steps.description: Design a watchdog feeding strategy that monitors all RTOS tasks, detecting any single stuck task even when others are healthy.

inputs.name: watchdog-config
inputs.desc: Watchdog type and timeout

inputs.name: system-timing
inputs.desc: Task list with expected cycle times

outputs.name: task-monitoring-design
outputs.desc: Check-in mechanism for each task, supervisor task logic, and the conditions that constitute a failure for each task

outputs.name: watchdog-feed-flow
outputs.desc: The exact code path from task check-ins through supervisor validation to watchdog feed, with no path that feeds the watchdog without verifying all tasks

process: Never feed the watchdog from a single point (like a timer ISR) because it will feed even when application tasks are stuck. Instead, implement a supervisor pattern: each task checks in by setting a flag or incrementing a counter, and a supervisor task verifies all tasks have checked in before feeding the watchdog.

Each task has a check-in deadline: the maximum time between consecutive check-ins. For periodic tasks, the deadline equals the period plus margin. For event-driven tasks, the deadline is the maximum expected idle time (or the task periodically checks in even when idle).

The supervisor task runs at the fastest task rate or on a timer. It reads each task's check-in counter, compares to the previous value, and resets the watchdog only if ALL tasks have checked in since the last supervisor cycle. If any task misses its deadline, the supervisor stops feeding the watchdog.

For tasks with variable execution time (e.g., a communication task that blocks on a receive), use a heartbeat within the blocking wait: the RTOS timeout on the blocking call should be shorter than the watchdog deadline, and the task sends a heartbeat (check-in) on each timeout, then retries the blocking call.

Handle task creation and deletion: when a task is created, register it with the supervisor (add to the monitored list). When a task is intentionally deleted, unregister it. The supervisor must not wait for check-ins from tasks that no longer exist.

steps.description: Implement runtime self-tests for CPU, RAM, flash, and clock monitoring as required by IEC 61508 and ISO 26262 for each safety integrity level.

inputs.name: task-monitoring-design
inputs.desc: Task supervision mechanism that self-tests integrate into

inputs.name: safety-requirements
inputs.desc: Target SIL/ASIL level determining required diagnostic coverage

outputs.name: self-test-suite
outputs.desc: Each test: what it checks, algorithm, execution time, frequency, and diagnostic coverage contribution

outputs.name: safe-state-transition
outputs.desc: For each detectable fault: the safe state to enter, the transition procedure, and the maximum time from detection to safe state

process: CPU register test: verify that each CPU register can hold all-zeros and all-ones without stuck bits. For ARM Cortex-M, test R0-R12, LR, PSP, MSP, APSR flags. Run at startup and periodically. Use a checkerboard pattern and its complement. Disable interrupts during the test to prevent register corruption by ISRs.

RAM test: use a march test algorithm (March C- provides good fault coverage with reasonable execution time). Test RAM in sections: copy the section to a backup area, run the march test, restore from backup. Do not test the section containing the test code's stack. Test each section periodically, rotating through all RAM over time.

Flash integrity test: compute CRC-32 over the flash contents and compare against a reference CRC stored at a known flash address (calculated at build time and embedded by the linker). Test the full image at startup. At runtime, test in sections to spread the CPU load: verify N pages per main-loop cycle, completing a full sweep every M seconds.

Clock monitoring: use the MCU's clock security system (CSS on STM32) to detect external oscillator failure and automatically switch to the internal RC oscillator. Additionally, cross-check the system clock against an independent time source: compare a timer clocked from the main oscillator against the RTC (clocked from LSE or LSI). A deviation beyond the expected tolerance indicates a clock fault.

Program flow monitoring: verify that the software executes the expected sequence of steps. Implement with a signature variable: each critical code block XORs a unique value into the signature. At a checkpoint, compare the signature against the expected value for that execution path. A wrong signature indicates that code was skipped, repeated, or corrupted.

Map each self-test to the fault model in IEC 61508 Table A.1 or ISO 26262 Part 5. Calculate the overall diagnostic coverage: DC = sum(coverage_i * failure_rate_i) / total_failure_rate. SIL 2 requires DC of at least 90%, SIL 3 requires 99%.

steps.description: Implement a question-and-answer watchdog protocol using an external watchdog IC for the highest diagnostic coverage in safety-critical systems.

inputs.name: self-test-suite
inputs.desc: Runtime self-tests that must pass before answering the watchdog

inputs.name: watchdog-config
inputs.desc: External watchdog IC specifications and communication interface

outputs.name: qa-watchdog-protocol
outputs.desc: Communication protocol with the external watchdog: seed exchange, response calculation, timing constraints, and error handling

outputs.name: safety-design-document
outputs.desc: Complete safety mechanism design: watchdog strategy, self-tests, diagnostic coverage calculation, and safe state definitions with verification plan

process: Select an external watchdog IC with Q&A capability (e.g., TI TPS3431, Infineon TLE9278). These ICs send a random seed to the MCU over SPI or a dedicated pin protocol. The MCU must compute the correct response (typically a CRC or polynomial calculation) and send it back within the timeout.

Integrate the Q&A exchange into the supervisor task flow: (1) all task check-ins verified, (2) all self-tests passed since last cycle, (3) read the seed from the watchdog IC, (4) compute the response, (5) send the response. If any step fails, do not respond, and the watchdog will reset the system.

The response calculation must be done by the application CPU, not a peripheral or DMA. This ensures the CPU is actually executing correct code. The calculation is typically a CRC or LFSR-based polynomial that is fast (under 100 us) but cannot be satisfied by a stuck value.

Handle the safe state transition: when the watchdog resets the system, the bootloader must check a flag or counter to determine if this was a watchdog reset (not a power-on reset). After N consecutive watchdog resets (e.g., 3), enter a permanent safe state (outputs de-energized, error indication active) rather than continuing to reset.

Document the complete safety design: fault model (what can go wrong), detection mechanism (which test or monitor catches it), reaction (safe state transition), and diagnostic coverage (per IEC 61508 or ISO 26262 methodology). This document is required for safety certification and must be maintained as the design evolves.

description: Systematic firmware debugging using JTAG/SWD, trace capabilities (ETM, ITM, DWT), hard fault analysis, timing measurement with logic analyzers, and post-mortem core dump analysis.

steps.description: Configure the debug probe (JTAG/SWD), target connection, and debug software for reliable access to the target's memory, registers, and execution state.

inputs.name: target-hardware
inputs.desc: MCU debug interface (JTAG/SWD pins), debug probe model, and IDE or command-line debugger being used

inputs.name: debug-requirements
inputs.desc: What needs to be debugged: crash analysis, timing issue, data corruption, or functional bug

outputs.name: debug-setup
outputs.desc: Probe connection verified, clock speed configured, flash algorithm loaded, and breakpoint/watchpoint capabilities confirmed

outputs.name: debug-strategy
outputs.desc: Which debug technique to use based on the symptom: breakpoints for functional bugs, watchpoints for memory corruption, trace for timing, post-mortem for field crashes

process: Verify the physical connection: SWD requires SWDIO, SWCLK, and GND (3 wires minimum). JTAG requires TDI, TDO, TMS, TCK, and GND (5 wires). SWD is preferred for ARM Cortex-M: fewer pins, same functionality for debugging. Connect the probe's VREF to the target's VDD so the probe knows the I/O voltage level.

Set the debug clock speed. Start at a conservative 1 MHz. Increase to 4 MHz or higher after confirming reliable communication. Long wires, high-capacitance boards, or noisy environments may require slower clocks. SWD at 10 MHz works on short, clean connections.

Load the correct flash programming algorithm for the MCU. The debugger needs this to program flash and set breakpoints in flash (flash breakpoints require patching the instruction, which means writing to flash). Hardware breakpoints (limited to 4 to 8 on Cortex-M) do not require flash writes.

Verify debugger features: confirm the number of hardware breakpoints and watchpoints available. Cortex-M3/M4 typically have 6 breakpoints and 4 watchpoints. Watchpoints can trigger on read, write, or read/write to a specific address or address range.

Choose the debug strategy based on the symptom. Reproducible functional bug: set breakpoints and step through. Intermittent data corruption: set a data watchpoint on the corrupted variable to catch the write. Timing issue: use ITM timestamps or GPIO toggling with a logic analyzer. Field crash: implement post-mortem core dump to flash.

steps.description: Use ARM CoreSight trace capabilities (ITM, DWT, ETM) for instrumented tracing, cycle-accurate profiling, and non-intrusive program flow monitoring.

inputs.name: debug-setup
inputs.desc: Working debug connection with trace port availability (SWO for ITM, or trace pins for ETM)

inputs.name: debug-strategy
inputs.desc: The specific information needed: execution timing, function call profile, data value trace, or interrupt timeline

outputs.name: trace-configuration
outputs.desc: ITM channels configured, DWT comparators set, SWO baud rate, and trace decoder settings

outputs.name: profiling-results
outputs.desc: Function execution times, interrupt latencies, CPU utilization breakdown, and cache hit rates (if applicable)

process: Configure ITM (Instrumentation Trace Macrocell) for printf-style debug output without halting the CPU. Write to the ITM stimulus port registers; the data streams out the SWO pin at the configured baud rate. This replaces UART printf debugging with near-zero overhead (1 cycle per word written).

Use DWT (Data Watchpoint and Trace) cycle counter for precise timing. Enable CYCCNT (cycle counter) at DWT_CTRL. Read DWT_CYCCNT before and after a code section. The difference divided by the clock frequency gives execution time with single-cycle precision. This is faster and more precise than GPIO toggling.

Configure DWT comparators for data trace: when a specific variable is written, DWT generates a trace packet containing the new value and timestamp. This captures the history of a variable without breakpoints and without stopping execution. Limited to 4 comparators.

For full program flow trace, configure ETM (Embedded Trace Macrocell) if the target supports it and a trace probe with the bandwidth is available. ETM captures every instruction execution and branches, allowing full reconstruction of the program flow. This requires a trace port (4-bit TPIU) and a high-bandwidth probe.
