Statistical profiling: sample the PC (program counter) periodically using DWT PC sampling. The distribution of PC values shows where the CPU spends its time. This is the embedded equivalent of a sampling profiler. Identify hot functions for optimization.

Decode the trace data using the IDE's trace viewer or a command-line tool. Map PC values to source code using the ELF file's debug symbols. Present the results as: function-level execution time breakdown, interrupt latency histogram, and timeline view of task switches.

steps.description: Analyze ARM Cortex-M hard faults by reading stacked registers, fault status registers, and reconstructing the call stack to identify the faulting instruction and root cause.

inputs.name: trace-configuration
inputs.desc: Available trace output for fault logging

inputs.name: debug-setup
inputs.desc: Debug connection for post-fault inspection

outputs.name: fault-analysis-procedure
outputs.desc: Step-by-step procedure to decode any hard fault: read registers, identify fault type, find faulting address, and determine root cause

outputs.name: fault-handler-implementation
outputs.desc: Hard fault handler code that captures all diagnostic information and either logs it or halts for debugger inspection

process: Implement a hard fault handler that captures the stacked register frame. On Cortex-M, the hardware pushes R0-R3, R12, LR, PC, and xPSR to the stack on exception entry. The stacked PC is the address of the faulting instruction (or the next instruction for some fault types). Read the MSP or PSP (check bit 2 of LR to determine which stack was active).

Read the fault status registers: HFSR (HardFault Status Register) tells if the fault was forced (escalated from another fault) or due to a vector table read error. CFSR (Configurable Fault Status Register) is split into MMFSR (memory management), BFSR (bus fault), and UFSR (usage fault) with specific bits for each fault cause.

Decode common fault causes: UFSR bit UNDEFINSTR = undefined instruction (corrupted code or branching to data). UFSR bit INVSTATE = attempt to execute ARM instructions on a Thumb-only core (function pointer without bit 0 set). BFSR bit PRECISERR + BFAR = bus error at the address in BFAR (reading unmapped memory). MMFSR bit DACCVIOL + MMFAR = MPU access violation at MMFAR.

Reconstruct the call stack from the fault context. Starting from the stacked LR (return address), walk the stack frame by frame. Each frame's LR points to the caller. Map addresses to function names using the ELF file: addr2line -e firmware.elf <address>. This shows the call chain that led to the fault.

In the fault handler, either halt for debugger inspection (infinite loop with the diagnostic data in registers/memory for the debugger to read) or log the fault data to a reserved RAM region / flash sector for post-mortem analysis. The choice depends on whether a debugger is attached (check the CoreDebug->DHCSR C_DEBUGEN bit).

steps.description: Implement post-mortem debugging for field-deployed devices: core dump to flash, stack unwinding from saved context, and remote diagnostic data retrieval.

inputs.name: fault-handler-implementation
inputs.desc: Fault handler that captures diagnostic data

inputs.name: fault-analysis-procedure
inputs.desc: Register and stack analysis procedure to apply to captured data

outputs.name: core-dump-implementation
outputs.desc: Code that saves registers, stack, and key memory regions to a dedicated flash sector on fault, with corruption protection and extraction interface

outputs.name: debug-methodology-document
outputs.desc: Complete debugging guide: probe setup, trace configuration, fault analysis, post-mortem, and a decision tree for which technique to use based on the symptom

process: Reserve a flash sector for the core dump. Size it for: stacked registers (32 bytes), fault status registers (12 bytes), full task stack contents (stack size, typically 1 KB to 4 KB), and selected global variables (application state, firmware version, uptime counter). Add a header with magic number, timestamp, and CRC for integrity.

In the fault handler: disable interrupts, write the header, write all captured registers, copy the active stack contents from the stack pointer to the stack base, write selected global state variables, compute and write the CRC, then enter the safe state (reset or halt).

Use the flash programming routines carefully in the fault handler: the flash driver itself may be corrupted if the fault was caused by code corruption. Use a minimal, self-contained flash write function that does not depend on any global state. Place it in a protected flash region.

Provide an extraction interface: at the next boot, the bootloader or application checks for a valid core dump in the reserved sector. If found, it can be read out via UART, USB, or a diagnostic protocol. Include the ELF file's build ID in the dump so the correct symbol file can be matched for analysis.

Analyze the extracted dump offline: load the registers and stack into GDB using the 'restore' command or a custom script. Use 'info frame' and 'backtrace' to reconstruct the call stack. Map the faulting PC to source code. Correlate the application state variables with the fault to determine the triggering condition.

Document the complete debug methodology: a decision tree starting from the symptom (crash, hang, wrong output, timing violation) through the appropriate technique (breakpoints, watchpoints, trace, post-mortem) to the root cause. Include worked examples of each common fault type.

description: Design a hardware abstraction layer for embedded firmware: register access patterns, peripheral driver architecture, DMA abstraction, pin mux management, clock tree configuration, and testing strategy for portability.

steps.description: Define the HAL layer structure: register access at the bottom, peripheral drivers in the middle, and board support package at the top, with clear interfaces between each.

inputs.name: target-mcus
inputs.desc: The set of MCUs the HAL must support (current target plus planned ports), with their register models and peripheral differences

inputs.name: portability-requirements
inputs.desc: Which peripherals must be portable across MCU families, and where platform-specific optimization is acceptable

outputs.name: layer-definitions
outputs.desc: Three layers defined: register access (CMSIS-level), peripheral driver (HAL API), and board support package (BSP), with the responsibility and interface of each

outputs.name: api-design-rules
outputs.desc: Rules for HAL API design: naming conventions, error handling pattern, callback registration, and what must be in the API vs what is configuration

process: Define three layers. Bottom: register access layer provides typed access to hardware registers. Use CMSIS-style header files with struct overlays for each peripheral (e.g., SPI_TypeDef with CR1, CR2, SR, DR members). This layer is MCU-specific and auto-generated from SVD files where possible.

Middle: peripheral driver layer provides a portable API. Functions like hal_spi_init(), hal_spi_transfer(), hal_spi_transfer_dma(). The API is the same across MCU families; the implementation behind it changes. This is where 90% of the porting effort lives.

Top: board support package (BSP) maps physical board resources to HAL objects. It defines which SPI peripheral instance connects to which device, which GPIO pins are used for chip selects, and the default configuration for each peripheral. The application code calls BSP functions (bsp_flash_spi_init()) which call HAL functions with the correct parameters.

Define the API contract: every HAL function returns a status code (HAL_OK, HAL_ERROR, HAL_BUSY, HAL_TIMEOUT). Callbacks are registered via function pointers, not hard-coded ISR names. Configuration is passed as a struct, not individual parameters, to allow future extension without breaking the API.

Separate compile-time configuration (which peripherals are enabled, buffer sizes) from runtime configuration (baud rate, mode). Compile-time config goes in a hal_conf.h header. Runtime config goes in the init struct. This allows dead-code elimination of unused peripherals.

steps.description: Implement the standard peripheral driver pattern: init/deinit lifecycle, enable/disable control, blocking and non-blocking transfer APIs, and interrupt/DMA callback integration.

inputs.name: layer-definitions
inputs.desc: HAL layer structure and responsibilities

inputs.name: api-design-rules
inputs.desc: API naming, error handling, and callback conventions

outputs.name: driver-template
outputs.desc: Complete driver template showing the standard pattern for any peripheral: handle struct, init, deinit, blocking ops, interrupt ops, DMA ops, and callback dispatch

outputs.name: state-machine-design
outputs.desc: Peripheral driver state machine: RESET -> READY -> BUSY_TX/BUSY_RX -> READY, with error states and recovery transitions

process: Define the peripheral handle struct. It contains: pointer to the peripheral registers (SPI_TypeDef*), configuration parameters (stored for reconfiguration), state (RESET/READY/BUSY/ERROR), DMA handles for TX and RX, callback function pointers, and a lock (to prevent concurrent access from task and ISR).

Implement the lifecycle: hal_spi_init() configures the peripheral registers from the config struct and transitions state from RESET to READY. hal_spi_deinit() disables the peripheral, releases DMA channels, and transitions to RESET. Init is idempotent (safe to call twice).

Implement three transfer modes. Blocking: hal_spi_transmit() polls the TX-empty flag and waits for completion with a timeout. Interrupt-driven: hal_spi_transmit_it() starts the transfer and returns immediately; the ISR sends each byte and calls the completion callback when done. DMA: hal_spi_transmit_dma() configures DMA and returns; the DMA-complete ISR calls the callback.

Implement the ISR dispatch: the peripheral's ISR reads the status register, clears flags, and calls the appropriate handler based on the current state (TX complete, RX complete, error). The handler updates the state machine and invokes the registered callback. The ISR function itself is MCU-specific; the handler logic is portable.

Handle concurrent access: use a simple lock (a state variable, not an RTOS mutex, since the driver must work without an RTOS). hal_spi_transmit() checks if state is READY before starting. If BUSY, return HAL_BUSY immediately. The application decides whether to retry, queue, or report the error.

steps.description: Abstract pin multiplexing and clock tree configuration so peripheral drivers do not contain pin or clock setup code, enabling board-level configuration without modifying drivers.

inputs.name: driver-template
inputs.desc: Standard driver pattern that needs pin and clock setup hooks

inputs.name: target-mcus
inputs.desc: MCU families with different pin mux and clock tree architectures

outputs.name: pin-mux-system
outputs.desc: Pin mux abstraction: pin definition struct, alternate function mapping, and the API for configuring a pin for a peripheral function

outputs.name: clock-tree-abstraction
outputs.desc: Clock tree configuration: system clock setup, peripheral clock enable/disable API, and frequency query API for baud rate calculation

process: Define a pin descriptor: port (GPIOA, GPIOB, ...), pin number (0-15), alternate function number (AF0-AF15 on STM32), pull-up/down, output speed, and drive strength. Store pin descriptors in the BSP, not the driver. The driver calls hal_gpio_init() with the pin descriptor during peripheral init.

Implement the alternate function mapping. On STM32, each pin has up to 16 alternate functions selected by the AFR registers. The BSP table maps each peripheral signal (SPI1_MOSI, UART2_TX) to a specific pin and AF number. This table is the only place that changes when a board revision moves a signal to a different pin.

Abstract clock enable: hal_rcc_periph_clock_enable(periph_id) enables the clock for the given peripheral. Internally, it sets the correct bit in the correct RCC enable register. The peripheral driver calls this in its init function, using a peripheral ID that the BSP provides.

Provide a clock frequency query: hal_rcc_get_pclk1_freq() returns the current APB1 bus clock frequency. Peripheral drivers use this to calculate baud rate divisors. This abstracts the clock tree so drivers do not need to know the PLL configuration or bus prescalers.

Handle low-power clock gating: hal_rcc_periph_clock_disable() in the deinit function. For sleep modes, provide hal_rcc_periph_clock_sleep_enable/disable() to control which peripheral clocks remain active during sleep. This allows the power management code to gate clocks without modifying each driver.

steps.description: Design a testing strategy for the HAL: unit testing on host with mocked registers, hardware-in-the-loop testing on target, and conformance testing across MCU families.

inputs.name: pin-mux-system
inputs.desc: Pin mux abstraction to be tested

inputs.name: clock-tree-abstraction
inputs.desc: Clock tree abstraction to be tested

outputs.name: test-architecture
outputs.desc: Three test levels: host unit tests (mocked registers), target integration tests (real hardware), and cross-platform conformance tests

outputs.name: hal-design-document
outputs.desc: Complete HAL specification: layer architecture, driver pattern, pin/clock abstraction, test strategy, and porting guide for adding a new MCU family

process: Host unit tests: replace the register access layer with a mock. The mock provides an array of uint32_t values representing each register. The driver code writes to these mock registers, and the test verifies the correct bits were set. This runs on the development machine with no hardware, testing the driver logic in isolation.

Create a register mock framework: a struct that mirrors the peripheral register layout, pre-initialized to reset values from the datasheet. After calling hal_spi_init(), assert that CR1 has the expected CPOL, CPHA, BR, and SPE bits. After calling hal_spi_transmit(), assert that DR was written with the correct data.

Target integration tests: run on the actual hardware with loopback connections (SPI MOSI connected to MISO, UART TX to RX, CAN with a single node and loopback mode). Verify that data transmitted is correctly received. Measure timing with GPIO toggling to confirm baud rates and latencies are within spec.

Cross-platform conformance tests: a test suite that runs the same test cases on every supported MCU family. The tests call only HAL API functions (not register-level code). If all conformance tests pass on a new MCU port, the port is considered functional. This is the acceptance criterion for porting.

Document the complete HAL design: layer responsibilities, the standard driver pattern with a worked example (SPI driver walkthrough), pin mux and clock abstraction APIs, the test strategy with example test cases, and a step-by-step porting guide for adding support for a new MCU family. The porting guide should specify exactly which files need to be created and which interfaces need to be implemented.

description: Test embedded firmware systematically: unit testing on host with hardware abstraction, hardware-in-the-loop fixture design, fixed-point math boundary testing, timing verification, CI regression with emulators, code coverage, and static analysis for MISRA compliance.

steps.description: Design unit tests that run on the host machine by abstracting hardware dependencies, using test doubles for peripherals, and testing algorithmic correctness in isolation.

inputs.name: firmware-architecture
inputs.desc: Code structure showing which modules depend on hardware and which are pure logic

inputs.name: test-framework-choice
inputs.desc: Unit test framework selection: Unity, CppUTest, Google Test, or cmocka, with rationale for the choice

outputs.name: test-doubles-design
outputs.desc: For each hardware-dependent module: the interface to mock, the mock implementation, and what the tests verify through the mock

outputs.name: unit-test-plan
outputs.desc: Test plan listing each module, its test cases, input ranges, expected outputs, and edge cases to cover

process: Separate firmware into testable layers: pure logic (algorithms, state machines, protocol parsers, data processing) that has no hardware dependency, and hardware interface code (register access, timing) that must be mocked. The pure logic layer should be the majority of the code.

Create test doubles (mocks/stubs) for hardware interfaces. A mock SPI driver stores the bytes 'transmitted' in an array and provides pre-loaded 'received' bytes. A mock GPIO records which pins were set/cleared. A mock timer returns pre-programmed tick values. The mock exposes inspection functions for test assertions.

Write tests for each pure-logic module. For a CAN message parser: test with valid messages (verify parsed signals match expected values), malformed messages (verify error handling), boundary values (signal at minimum, maximum, and one-bit-off), and byte-order edge cases.

For state machines, test every transition: feed inputs that trigger each valid transition and verify the resulting state and outputs. Feed inputs for invalid transitions and verify the state machine stays in the current state and reports the error. Use a state transition coverage metric.

Compile and run on the host using the native compiler (GCC or Clang for x86/x64). The firmware code includes the HAL headers that resolve to mocks in the test build and to real hardware in the target build. This requires the abstraction layer to be clean: no #include of MCU-specific headers in testable code.

steps.description: Design hardware-in-the-loop test fixtures that exercise the firmware on real hardware with controlled stimuli and automated result verification.

inputs.name: unit-test-plan
inputs.desc: Unit tests covering logic; HIL tests now need to cover hardware interaction

inputs.name: test-doubles-design
inputs.desc: Interfaces that were mocked in unit tests and now need real hardware testing

outputs.name: hil-fixture-design
outputs.desc: Test fixture schematic: target board connections, stimulus generation (signal generators, CAN adapters, SPI masters), measurement (logic analyzers, oscilloscopes, current sensors), and test host interface

outputs.name: hil-test-cases
outputs.desc: Test cases that can only be verified with real hardware: timing, interrupt behavior, power consumption, and communication with real peripherals

process: Define the HIL fixture hardware. Minimum: the device under test (DUT), a test host (PC or Raspberry Pi), a debug probe for flashing and control, and a bus interface for each communication protocol (USB-to-CAN adapter, USB-to-SPI, USB-to-UART). Add signal conditioning as needed (level shifters, attenuators).

Automate stimulus generation: the test host sends scripted commands over each communication interface. For CAN: send specific message IDs with known payloads and verify the DUT's response messages. For analog inputs: use a DAC connected to the DUT's ADC input to inject known voltages.

Automate result verification: the test host reads the DUT's outputs (GPIO states via a logic analyzer, CAN response messages, UART output) and compares against expected values. Use GPIO pins on the DUT as test points: the firmware toggles them at key events, and the test host captures the timing.

Design power measurement into the fixture: a current sense amplifier (INA219 or similar) on the DUT's supply rail, readable by the test host over I2C. This allows automated power consumption tests: verify that sleep mode current is below the spec, active mode current matches the power budget.

Create a test sequencer that runs the full HIL suite: flash the firmware, wait for boot, execute each test case, collect results, generate a pass/fail report. The sequencer must handle DUT resets (via the debug probe or a relay on the power supply) for tests that require a clean start.

steps.description: Test fixed-point math implementations for overflow, underflow, rounding errors, and precision loss at boundary values.

inputs.name: hil-test-cases
inputs.desc: Hardware-level tests; this flow adds algorithmic boundary tests for fixed-point code

inputs.name: firmware-architecture
inputs.desc: Modules using fixed-point arithmetic with their Q formats and value ranges

outputs.name: fixed-point-test-suite
outputs.desc: Test cases for each fixed-point operation: inputs at boundaries, expected outputs calculated in floating-point, and maximum acceptable error (ULP count)

outputs.name: precision-analysis
outputs.desc: For each fixed-point calculation chain: accumulated error from input to output, identifying where precision loss occurs and whether it affects the application

process: Identify all fixed-point operations in the firmware. For each, document the Q format (e.g., Q15 = 16-bit signed with 15 fractional bits, range -1.0 to +0.999969). List the operations: add, subtract, multiply (with shift), divide, and any conversions between Q formats.

For each operation, define boundary test values. Addition: both operands at maximum positive (overflow), both at maximum negative (underflow), one at max positive and one at max negative (should not overflow). Multiplication in Q15: 0x7FFF * 0x7FFF must not overflow the intermediate 32-bit result before the shift.

Calculate expected outputs using double-precision floating-point as the reference. Convert the fixed-point input to float, perform the operation, convert back to fixed-point. The maximum acceptable error is the quantization step size (1 ULP = 2^-Q where Q is the fractional bits). Most operations should be within 1 ULP; chained operations may accumulate to 2 or 3 ULP.

Test saturation behavior: if the firmware uses saturating arithmetic (clips to max/min instead of wrapping), verify that overflow produces the maximum representable value, not a wrapped-around value. If using wrapping arithmetic, verify the firmware checks for overflow before the operation.

Trace precision through calculation chains: a PID controller with Q15 coefficients multiplied by Q15 error, accumulated in Q31, and shifted back to Q15 output. Each step introduces up to 1 ULP error. A 10-step chain can accumulate 10 ULP, which in Q15 is 10/32768 = 0.03%. Verify this is within the application's tolerance.

steps.description: Set up continuous integration for embedded firmware with emulator-based regression testing, code coverage measurement, and automated quality gates.

inputs.name: fixed-point-test-suite
inputs.desc: Algorithmic tests to include in the CI pipeline

inputs.name: unit-test-plan
inputs.desc: Host-based unit tests to include in the CI pipeline

outputs.name: ci-pipeline-design
outputs.desc: CI stages: compile, static analysis, unit tests, emulator tests, coverage report, and quality gate criteria for each stage

outputs.name: coverage-targets
outputs.desc: Code coverage targets: line coverage, branch coverage, and MC/DC coverage (for safety-critical code), with the rationale for each target

process: Set up the CI build: cross-compile the firmware for the target (ARM GCC) and native-compile for host tests (x86 GCC/Clang). The cross-compile verifies the firmware builds without errors or warnings (-Wall -Werror). The native compile builds the test executables.

Run unit tests on every commit. The CI runner executes the host-based test suite and reports pass/fail. Test execution is fast (seconds) because it runs natively. Fail the pipeline on any test failure.

For emulator-based testing, use QEMU with the target MCU's machine model (available for many ARM Cortex-M families) or a vendor-provided simulator. Flash the firmware into the emulator, run the test sequence, and capture the output. Emulator tests are slower but test the actual target binary including startup code and peripheral interaction (with emulated peripherals).

Measure code coverage: compile with --coverage (GCC) to instrument the code. Run the tests. Use gcov to generate coverage data and lcov/genhtml for HTML reports. For embedded targets, use semihosting to extract the gcov data files from the target to the host after test execution.

Set quality gates: line coverage at least 80% for application code (not bootloader or HAL), branch coverage at least 70%. For safety-critical code (SIL 3+), require MC/DC (Modified Condition/Decision Coverage) at 100% for safety-related modules. MC/DC means every condition in every decision has been shown to independently affect the outcome.

steps.description: Configure static analysis tools for MISRA C compliance, define the rule set for the project, handle deviations, and integrate into the CI pipeline.

inputs.name: ci-pipeline-design
inputs.desc: CI pipeline to add static analysis stage

inputs.name: firmware-architecture
inputs.desc: Code modules with their safety criticality classification

outputs.name: misra-configuration
outputs.desc: MISRA C:2012 rule selection (mandatory, required, advisory), tool configuration (PC-lint, Polyspace, cppcheck, or Parasoft), and suppression/deviation policy

outputs.name: testing-methodology-document
outputs.desc: Complete testing strategy: unit tests, HIL, fixed-point, CI, coverage, static analysis, and the traceability from requirements through tests to coverage evidence

process: Select the MISRA C:2012 rule set. All 10 mandatory rules must be enforced with zero deviations. The 143 required rules should be enforced with documented deviations where necessary. The 30 advisory rules: enable the ones relevant to the project (pointer arithmetic, implicit conversions, side effects in macros) and document why others are excluded.

Configure the static analysis tool. For open-source: cppcheck with MISRA addon provides good coverage of required rules. For commercial: PC-lint Plus or Polyspace provide higher coverage and fewer false positives. Configure the tool to use the project's target compiler settings (data type sizes, endianness, alignment) for accurate analysis.

Handle deviations: when a required rule must be violated (e.g., Rule 11.3 prohibits pointer casts, but register access requires casting integer addresses to pointers), document the deviation: which rule, where in the code, why the deviation is necessary, and what mitigation ensures safety (e.g., the cast is in a controlled macro used only for register access).

Integrate into CI: run static analysis on every commit. New violations added by the commit fail the pipeline. Existing violations (in the baseline) are tracked but do not fail the build. The baseline shrinks over time as violations are fixed. This prevents regression while allowing gradual improvement.

Document the complete testing methodology: traceability from each requirement to the test(s) that verify it, the test level (unit/integration/system/HIL), the coverage evidence, and the static analysis clean report. This document is required for safety certification (IEC 61508, ISO 26262) and serves as the verification summary for the project.
